Ranked-RMSPE permutation p-value for a synthetic control

Source: R/rmspe_pvalue.R
rmspe_pvalue.Rd

The inference Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller propose and Orlova, Rury and Wiltshire (2023) use: fit the same synthetic control with each donor standing in as the treated unit, rank the treated unit's ratio of post-treatment to pre-treatment RMSPE against that distribution, and report the rank as a fraction of the units.

Usage

rmspe_pvalue(
  ratio,
  att,
  treated,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "greater", "less")
)

Arguments

ratio

Numeric vector of RMSPE ratios, one per unit – the rmspe_ratio element of fit_scm(), for the treated unit and every in-space placebo. Named, ideally.

att

Numeric vector of estimated effects in the same order, used only to sign the statistic for a one-sided test.

treated

Index or name identifying the treated unit within ratio.

alternative

"two.sided" (default), "greater" or "less".

Value

A list with p_value, rank (the treated unit's rank, 1 being the most extreme), n_units, statistic (the treated unit's signed or unsigned ratio), floor (1 / n_units), and alternative.

Details

Dividing by the pre-period RMSPE is what makes the statistic comparable across units: a placebo that never had a good synthetic control in the first place has a large post-period gap for reasons that have nothing to do with treatment, and the ratio nets that out. Poorly fitting placebos are therefore kept, not trimmed – trimming them is what would make the test anti-conservative.

What one-sided means here

The RMSPE ratio is unsigned, so a two-sided test can rank it directly. A one-sided test needs the sign back: the statistic becomes sign(att) * ratio, so a placebo that moved hard in the opposite direction to the hypothesised effect ranks below the treated unit rather than beside it. Where the direction of any effect is genuinely known in advance, this is a real power gain with a small number of donors; where it is not, "two.sided" is the honest default and is what this function does unless told otherwise.

The floor, which matters with few donors

The smallest attainable p-value is 1/n_units: even a treated unit that out-ranks every placebo gets 1/n, never zero. With 40 units that floor is 0.025, and a p-value of 0.05 means "second largest of forty", not "significant at five percent" in the usual sampling sense. Read these as ranks, and do not report them to three decimals as if they were continuous.

See also

fit_scm(), and scm_placebo_permutation() which produces the vectors this takes.

Examples

rmspe_pvalue(c(wm = 6.2, a = 1.1, b = 2.0, c = 0.7),
             att = c(28.9, -2, 4, 1), treated = "wm")
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.25
#> 
#> $rank
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_units
#> [1] 4
#> 
#> $statistic
#> [1] 6.2
#> 
#> $floor
#> [1] 0.25
#> 
#> $alternative
#> [1] "two.sided"
#>
